To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in Pearson cells with a heteroplsmic deletion of mtDNA a reduced expression of mtDNA-encoded genes does not result in a decreased activity of the corresponding mitochondrial enzymes, because of the overproduction of the nuclearly encoded subunits.
in lymphoblastoid cells the mitochondrial phenotype is normal despite a severe reduction in the expression of one (or more) mitochondrial genes.

the relationship between mitochondrial genotype (the percentage of deleted mtDNA) and mitochondrial phenotype (the expression of mtDNA-encoded subunits of oxidative phosphorylation) depends on the relative amounts of the subunits of the enzymes involved.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the genotype and phenotype of the mitochondrial genome

the relationship between mitochondrial genotype (i.e. the amount and type of mutated mtDNA) and mitochondrial phenotype (i.e. how much energy is produced and how well mitochondria function) in lymphoblast cells.
the relationship between mitochondrial genotype (the amount of deleted mtDNA) and phenotype (the expression of mitochondrial genes) in a lymphoblastoid cell line derived from a Pearson patient.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in the Pearson syndrome, a deletion of 5 kb from the COX II to ND5 gene leads to an intermediate reduction of the mtDNA-encoded subunits of cytoplasmic enzymes involved in oxidative metabolism, which is compensated by an overproduction of the nuclearly encoded subunits of these enzymes.

the relationship between mitochondrial genotype (the percentage of deleted mtDNA) and the mitochondrial phenotype (the capacity for oxidative phosphorylization) is complex and depends on a number of parameters.

the expression of a mitochondrial genome with a large heteroplasmic deletion can be severely reduced, but that a reduction in mitochondrial gene expression does not necessarily lead to a reduced mitochondrial function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a mitochondrial phenotype is not necessarily related to the mitochondrial genotype.
the expression of mitochondrial genes can be severely reduced without any obvious consequences for mitochondrial function.
the mitochondrial genotype and the mitochondrial phenotype are not always related.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the relationship between mitochondrial genotype (i.e. the proportion of deleted mtDNA) and mitochondrial phenotype (i.e. expression of mitochondrial genes and mitochondrial function) is not necessarily linear.
the mitochondrial genotype does not always predict the mitochondrial phenotype.

the expression of mitochondrial genes is regulated in a tissue-specific manner and that a reduction in expression of mitochondrial genes does not necessarily result in a reduction in the function of the corresponding mitochondrial enzymes.
